title: Kim et al. (2015): Professor Question Practice
instructions: Practice a 30-second response: state your conclusion, distinguish concepts, and connect a cited example or statistic with its limits. Keep countries, sample denominators, and historical contexts distinct, and label family or policy applications as inferences.

cards.title: State the chapter's central conclusion in one sentence.
cards.answer_30s: Asian families are adapting to changing socioeconomic conditions by renegotiating traditional filial beliefs and forms of intergenerational support. Evidence about declining support is mixed, and both practices and beliefs vary. The chapter argues that culturally sensitive research should examine multiple aspects of parent-child relationships from both generations' perspectives, rather than reduce change to a single measure of filial decline.

cards.title: What does the chapter mean by the paradox of filial piety?
cards.answer_30s: Strong beliefs about supporting and respecting parents may coexist with changing contact and assistance. In a Beijing university study, 89% endorsed financial support for parents as a criterion of adulthood. A separate Chinese survey reported in 2012 found that 33% saw parents only annually and 12% had not visited for years. These are different studies, so they do not demonstrate an attitude-behavior contradiction within the same individuals.

cards.title: How does the chapter contrast filial piety with Western filial responsibility?
cards.answer_30s: Both include supporting older parents, but filial piety also emphasizes how help is given: respect, gratitude, obedience, protecting parents' face, and bringing them honor. It describes a lifelong responsibility that includes healthy parents, while the chapter characterizes Western filial responsibility as more focused on helping when needs arise. These are contrasting emphases in the literature, rather than traits present in every member of one culture and absent in another.

cards.title: Why distinguish normative from functional solidarity?
cards.answer_30s: Normative solidarity concerns beliefs that children should help parents; functional solidarity concerns actual exchanges of help, money, time, or care. A belief measure therefore cannot substitute for observed support. The chapter also warns that studies use inconsistent definitions of filial piety. Treating coresidence or care alone as the whole concept can obscure motivations and the gap between norms and behavior.

cards.title: Explain the two dimensions and value of the Dual Filial Piety Model.
cards.answer_30s: Reciprocal filial piety centers on love, care, and gratitude for parents' sacrifices and investment. Authoritarian filial piety centers on hierarchy, parental authority, and obedience attached to the child's role, potentially suppressing personal wishes. Distinguishing these dimensions can reveal simultaneous continuity and change: younger adults may retain support obligations while giving parents less authority over career or marriage decisions.

cards.title: Why is modernization alone insufficient to explain family change?
cards.answer_30s: Modernization theory predicts weaker extended-family obligations with industrialization and urbanization. But the chapter shows that policies and historical context also matter. In a comparison using 1990s data, adults in Taiwan endorsed some more traditional beliefs than those in mainland China despite Taiwan's greater economic development. Change therefore cannot be assumed to follow a uniform path of Westernization or declining filial commitment.

cards.title: How can government policy shape filial behavior?
cards.answer_30s: The chapter describes China's Family Support Agreements as seeking legally enforceable financial and practical assistance. It contrasts these with national long-term care insurance introduced in Japan in 2000 and South Korea in 2008 to address care gaps. Such policies can strengthen safety nets while changing family roles. The authors also raise possible unintended effects on spontaneity, flexibility, affection, and trust, rather than establish that public provision simply replaces family support.

cards.title: Give examples of filial piety taking new forms.
cards.answer_30s: In rural China, ritualistic coresidence involves briefly living in the paternal household after marriage to express filial commitment. For some Chinese Singaporean parents, an open invitation to coreside can fulfill the traditional ideal even without moving in. Paying for high-quality institutional care when direct care is impractical is another reinterpretation. The chapter notes that access to some of these new practices may depend on social class.

cards.title: How should we interpret the cited coresidence percentages?
cards.answer_30s: The chapter cites separate studies reporting coresidence with adult children among older adults aged 65 or over: 14% in the United States, 43% in Japan, and 68.7% in China. These historical estimates illustrate differing living arrangements, rather than rank filial virtue or care quality. Living together can facilitate support, but does not automatically guarantee good care or better relationships.

cards.title: What is quasi-coresidence, and what are its limits?
cards.answer_30s: Quasi-coresidence means separate households located nearby. In a cited Chinese study, among parents aged 60 or over who had children and lived alone or only with a spouse, 59% had a child in the same village or community and 79% in the same county. A Korean study nevertheless associated nearby separate residence with more depressive symptoms than coresidence. Proximity alone therefore does not establish supportive interaction or better well-being.

cards.title: Why view intergenerational coresidence as mutual aid?
cards.answer_30s: Coresidence can respond to parental widowhood or poor health, but also to adult children's housing and childcare needs. Older parents may provide housing or grandchild care while children provide money and assistance. The chapter therefore frames living arrangements through both generations' needs, resources, and negotiations. They are not adequately explained as one-way parental dependence or a direct measure of children's filial commitment.

cards.title: What shows that living apart need not mean support has stopped?
cards.answer_30s: Non-coresident children can live nearby, maintain contact, and provide money. A Korean study cited as Park (2012) reported that 57% of older parents had in-person contact at least monthly and 89% had phone or email contact. Migrant children could also send more money to compensate for less hands-on care. Residential separation can constrain daily help without eliminating other exchanges.

cards.title: Why are findings on children's support and parental well-being mixed?
cards.answer_30s: Many studies are cross-sectional: parents in poor health or well-being may receive more help, making need-driven support look harmful. The meaning of help can also depend on culturally expected providers and beliefs such as familism. These design and contextual differences can produce inconsistent associations. A correlation alone cannot establish the causal effect of receiving support.

cards.title: Why measure emotional closeness in culturally sensitive ways?
cards.answer_30s: Studies reviewed in the chapter suggest that some Asian adults are reluctant to request emotional support explicitly because they fear worrying others, disrupting harmony, or losing face. Fewer direct requests or fewer relatives named as intimate therefore need not mean that family ties matter less or are lower quality. Research should distinguish forms of emotional expression from relationship quality and consider less explicit forms of support.

cards.title: What is intergenerational ambivalence, and how do its two levels differ?
cards.answer_30s: Ambivalence means positive and negative sentiments toward the same parent-child relationship, such as affection alongside burden or conflict. Structural ambivalence concerns competing social roles and expectations, for example paid employment alongside gendered care obligations. Psychological ambivalence concerns a person's mixed feelings toward a particular relative. The levels may be connected, but contradictory role demands and subjective feelings are not identical measures.

reading_response.title: Practice Answering: How Did You Read This Chapter?
reading_response.instructions: Connect the main claim, memorable evidence, conceptual distinctions, and limitations in your own words. Keep historical examples in context and identify family or policy implications as inferences.

cards.title: A 30-second overall response
cards.answer_30s: I read this chapter as showing how families renegotiate support and filial expectations under changing socioeconomic conditions, rather than simply deciding whether support in Asia is declining. The evidence is mixed across beliefs and forms of assistance. I found its call to consider both parents' and children' perspectives especially important for understanding change without imposing a single cultural standard.

cards.title: Which paradox stood out to you?
cards.answer_30s: I was struck by the strong norm illustrated by 89% of Beijing university students endorsing parental financial support as a marker of adulthood, alongside a separate Chinese survey reporting that 33% visited only annually. Because these are different samples, I would not claim that the same people contradicted their beliefs. I read the contrast as a reason to investigate how norms and practices may move differently.

cards.title: How did your previous view change?
cards.answer_30s: I had pictured coresidence mainly as older parents in poor health depending on adult children. The chapter also describes children's housing and childcare needs and older parents' contributions of housing and grandchild care. That changed my view toward mutual aid: both generations' resources and needs help explain the arrangement, rather than parental need alone.

cards.title: Why did you stop treating filial piety as one norm?
cards.answer_30s: The Dual Filial Piety Model made a single strong-versus-weak scale seem insufficient to me. Gratitude and loving repayment of parental investment differ from obedience rooted in hierarchy and role obligations. This distinction helps explain why support duties can remain valued even when deference over jobs or marriage declines. I would ask which dimension is changing before claiming that filial piety as a whole has weakened.

cards.title: What interpretive limitation stood out to you?
cards.answer_30s: I would not turn the separate US, Japanese, and Chinese coresidence estimates of 14%, 43%, and 68.7% into a ranking of filial piety or care quality. These are historical figures from different cited studies, and the chapter itself warns against equating high coresidence with adequate care. Support can cross households, while shared residence can coexist with poor care or conflict.

cards.title: How would you connect the chapter to families or policy?
cards.answer_30s: My inference is to evaluate how policies interact with family relationships, as well as whether they secure care. The chapter contrasts legally enforceable Family Support Agreements in China with long-term care insurance in Japan and South Korea. It raises the possibility that sanctions could weaken flexibility, affection, or trust. I would treat these as potential consequences to investigate, rather than assume that government support necessarily replaces family commitment.
